title: Object-Oriented Modelling
intro: What OO is, compared with procedural code: objects, classes, the four OO concepts, and how Java gets from source code to a running program. Every later chapter builds on these words.

cards.title: Two ways to organise a program
cards.body:
**Procedural programming** (C, Pascal, Fortran): a program is a list of step-by-step instructions grouped into **functions**, all reading and changing shared (often global) data.

**Object-oriented programming** (Java, C++, C#, Smalltalk): the program is a set of **objects**. Each object bundles its own data with the methods that change it. Work gets done by objects **sending messages** to each other.

cards.body: The slides group languages by paradigm. Know which group each one belongs to.

cards.after: C++ is **not pure OOP**: it is a superset of C, so you can write C++ with no classes at all. Java forces everything into classes. Even `main` lives inside a class.
keypoints: Procedural = imperative: statements, assignments, step-by-step
C++ = C + OO features, but optional (not pure OO)
Java: no pointers, no multiple inheritance (of classes)

cards.title: What is an object?
cards.body:
An object is one specific thing. It has three characteristics:
**Identity**: which one it is. Every object is unique, even if its values match another object's.
**State**: its attribute values right now.
**Behaviour**: what it can do (its methods).

cards.title: Class vs object
cards.body:
A **class** is the blueprint (template). It says which attributes and methods every object of that kind has. An **object** is one **instance** made from the class, holding its own values. *Person* is a class. *Obama* is an object of class Person.

In UML, an object's name is **underlined**: `bill : Person`.

cards.title: Four basic components + message passing
cards.body:
The slides' OO model has four basic components:
**Objects**: hold state plus actions.
**Messages**: a request from one object to another to produce some result.
**Methods**: what an object does when it receives a message.
**Classes**: the template that objects belong to.

In Java, `rect.findArea()` **sends the message** `findArea` to the receiver object `rect`.
cards.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant d as app:Driver
  participant r as rect:Rectangle
  d->>r: findArea()
  activate r
  Note over r: method runs on r's own data
  r-->>d: 50.0
  deactivate r
keypoints: Message = request, method = how the receiver responds
Syntax: receiver.method(arguments)
The sender only needs to know WHAT to ask

cards.title: Abstraction
cards.body:
Booch's definition: an abstraction denotes the **essential characteristics** of an object that distinguish it from all other kinds of objects, **relative to the perspective of the viewer**.

Keep only what matters to your problem. A rectangle in a drawing app needs only `width` and `height`, plus `findArea()` and `findPerimeter()`. The client sees the behaviour on its side of the **abstraction barrier**.

cards.title: Encapsulation vs information hiding
cards.body:
The slides keep the two apart:
**Encapsulation** builds a **barrier** that protects an object's private data. You reach that data only through the object's **public methods** (get/set).
**Information hiding** hides the **implementation details** from users. They need to know only *what* a class does and *how to call* it, not how the methods work inside.

Coke machine: you may call `getACoke()`, but you cannot call `getRecipe()`.

cards.title: Inheritance
cards.body: Inheritance defines a new class (the **subclass**, derived class or child) that inherits the attributes and methods of an existing class (the **superclass**, base class or parent). The subclass can **add** new attributes and methods and can **redefine (override)** inherited ones. It gives you reuse without copying code. Test for it with **"is a / is an"**: an HourlyEmployee *is an* Employee.
cards.after: SalariedEmployee **adds** `weeklySalary` and `overtimePay()`. HourlyEmployee **overrides** `earnings()`. Both still have firstName, lastName and socialSecurityNo.
keypoints: Superclass = base = parent; subclass = derived = child
Subclass inherits, can add, can override
Relationship: 'is a'

cards.title: Multiple inheritance (and why Java avoids it)
cards.body:
**Multiple inheritance** means one class has more than one superclass. The problem: if both parents have a `name` or the same method, which one does the child inherit? The slides list three fixes: user-specified precedence (Smalltalk), renaming one of them, or keeping both when their signatures differ.

**Java does not allow** a class to extend two classes. `class StudentEmployee extends Student, Employee` is a compile error.
cards.diagram:
classDiagram
  class Student {
    name
    age
    printExamRes()
  }
  class Employee {
    name
    age
    salary
    earnings()
  }
  Student <|-- StudentEmployee
  Employee <|-- StudentEmployee
keypoints: Conflict: same member in both parents
Java: one superclass per class (single inheritance)
C++ allows multiple inheritance

cards.title: Polymorphism
cards.body: Polymorphism comes from the Greek for "many forms". The **same message** can be sent to different objects, and **each responds in the way that suits its own class**. The sender does not need to know the receiver's exact class. The slides call it the most powerful OO concept.
keypoints: Same message, different behaviour per class
The sender is unaware of the receiver's class
Add a new subclass and call() needs no change

cards.title: The Java pipeline: compile time vs run time
cards.body:
**Step 1, compile time:** `javac Hello.java` translates source into **bytecode** in `Hello.class`. Bytecode is not machine code for any real CPU.
**Step 2, run time:** `java Hello` starts the **JVM**. Its **class loader** loads the .class file. The **interpreter** runs the bytecode, and the **JIT compiler** turns frequently used (hot) bytecode into native **machine code**.

cards.title: C vs Java: where the code lives
cards.body: In C, functions and global variables sit loose in a file, and `main` is a free function. In Java, **everything lives inside a class**: attributes, methods and even `main`. A public class `Factorial` must be saved as `Factorial.java`.
keypoints: Java has no global variables or free functions
public class X goes in X.java
main is static and lives inside a class

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body:
**1. "The JIT compiles .java to .class."** No. That is javac. The JIT works at run time on bytecode.
**2. "The JRE contains the JDK."** No, the other way round: JDK contains JRE contains JVM.
**3. "Encapsulation and information hiding are identical."** The slides separate them: encapsulation is the barrier (private data, public methods), and information hiding hides the implementation.
**4. "A class is an object."** A class is the template. Objects are instances made from it.
**5. "Polymorphism means overloading."** In Chapter 1 it means the same message gets a different response per class.
keypoints: Pipeline order: javac, then .class, then JVM (loader, interpreter/JIT)
Identity is unique even when two objects have equal state
Inheritance = is-a
